doc.title: Steve Allen interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, February 15, 1999

title: Longevity of musicians and Allen's own playing and composing at 77
summary: Allen says jazz players can improve with age and that he is a better composer now.

story.theme_name: Late-career reflections: awards, legacy and life lessons
story.community_name: Looking back: no regrets, what it all meant

blocks.x: I love the longevity that’s possible in music too, with the players.
I feel sorry for dancers sometimes, they have a certain point that they can get to but some of our greatest players —

A very wise observation on your part. The same thing is true of actors, depending on the kind of acting they do, time can be cruel to them. If what they chiefly market, if what chiefly explains their success is their physical beauty or handsomeness, they’re not always going to have it. But you can be 74 years old and be playing jazz probably better than you did at 54 or 24. You know more. And I used to think that at least you would lose your chops you know, your technical facility as you got old, but I’m now 77 and I play at least as good at this age as I did at any earlier age. So speaking personally I haven’t lost © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -22-

anything. In fact as a composer I am considerably better now than back when I was writing a lot of my songs that were hits. Because you don’t have to be Beethoven, as we’ve already established, to write a popular song. But harmonically I’m much more advanced now and so I’m writing more unusual melodies, despite my age.
